pages.transcript:
We strongly believe that something must be done to correct this situation. During at least one meeting with staff members, you indicated that you would be evaluating the salary situation and addressing past inequities. We support such an effort.

In addition, we have two requests:

*That the salaries of black female employees be adjusted to levels that equal the salaries of white male employees who have the same amount of experience and are in comparable positions.

*That newly hired black female employees who are fully experienced receive salaries equal to those of newly hired white males who are fully experienced.

We make these requests in a sincere effort to end the financial inequity for those of us who are black and female. We look forward to your response.

Sincerely,

documents.subject: Employer/settlement narrative comparing salaries of Michael O'Harrow and Steve Pearlstein to Hamilton and Mayer; experience, education, and starting-salary sections

pages.transcript:
CONFIDENTIAL INFORMATION UNDER THE AGREED ARBITRATION PROCEDURES
PREPARED FOR SETTLEMENT PURPOSES

Salary History
As of September 1, 2002, O'Harrow received three merit increases — two of which he received as a reporter in Financial News. He received these two merit increases in 2000 and 2001. When he returned from the Investigative Unit in 2000, O'Harrow received an approximately 70 percent salary increase, making his salary substantially more than the salaries of Hamilton and Mayer at that time.

Explanation:
O'Harrow is considered an expert in digital privacy and was a finalist for the Pulitzer Prize three years ago.

Because O'Harrow was highly valued because of his expertise, he was put on the fast-track. O'Harrow also received an approximately 70 percent salary increase when he returned from the Investigative Unit to Financial News.

O'Harrow had a substantial number of high impact A1 stories.

Steve Pearlstein

Steve Pearlstein was paid more than Walsh on the 1992 to 1997 salary snapshots, except he was paid slightly more on the 1995 salary snapshot (Walsh does not appear on the 2000 to 2002 salary snapshots — Pearlstein does not appear on the 1999 and 2000 salary snapshots).

Experience and Education
Pearlstein came to The Post in the late 1980s as the Deputy Editor in Financial News, a position he held for roughly three years before becoming a reporter in Financial News in 1991. He became a foreign correspondent in the Canada Bureau in 1998, returning to Financial News as a reporter in 2000, where he remains today. Prior to starting at The Post, Pearlstein worked as a Senior Editor at Inc. Magazine for approximately two and-a-half years. He also founded The Boston Observer where he served as its Editor and Publisher for approximately three years. He also worked at the Concord Monitor for two years and Foster's Daily Democrat for one year. Lastly, Pearlstein served as a writer, on-air reporter and Acting Managing Editor of WGBH-TV for approximately three years. Pearlstein is a graduate of Trinity College in Hartford, Connecticut.

Starting Salary
Upon starting at The Post, Pearlstein received approximately a 17 percent increase over his prior salary at Inc. Magazine. His starting salary was substantially more than the salary of Walsh at that time.

pages.transcript:
ASSISTANT EDITORS,
ASSIGNMENT EDITORS & MAKE-UP
HOW OTHER SALARIES COMPARE TO WHITE MALE AVERAGE SALARIES, 1982 & 1986

[Chart: y-axis 'WHAT WHITE MALES AVERAGE' from -2 to -10; panel WHITE FEMALES: bars -5.5% (1982), -8.6% (1986); panel ALL BLACKS: bars -4.9% (1982), -4.8% (1986)]

WHY DOES THE POST DISCRIMINATE?

We don't think that the Post has a conscious policy of discrimination but it discriminates.

We don't think most managers and supervisors at the Post discriminate consciously on the basis of race and sex. But conscious or unconscious, the results are the same.

The salary system that the Post created and maintains allows discrimination to do its work.

A major cause of the discrimination in pay is the multi-tier wage system. The system began in the late 1970s when there was no contract in effect. During that time and the Post unilaterally handed out pay increases. When the Post finally settled on a contract three years later, those pay increases were not incorporated in the contractual rates of pay. As a result, people who had been on the payroll before the contract was signed had higher salaries than those who were hired later. That pattern was extended — at the Post's insistence — in the contract signed in 1979 and in the current contract.

In the late 1960s and early 1970s, blacks and women faced another kind of discrimination. They could not get hired for the better paying jobs here. The Post has made progress since then in hiring more women and minorities. But it also set up a pay system that favors employees who worked at the Post before 1976. Among reporters and editors, outside advertising sales staff, top-ranked computer programmers and in other better paying jobs, that means white males. Since then the Post has hired an increasing number of blacks and women — but at lower salaries.

But that's not the only way in which The Post discriminates. To try to determine whether the patterns in salaries were entirely the effect of differences in longevity which favor white males, we looked at the salaries of all fully experienced reporters hired in a single contract year within the past two years—all hired as "journeymen" reporters, all hired by the Post at approximately the same time.

The results? Fully experienced white males hired that year now are paid an average of $1046.68. Black males hired that year and rated as fully experienced now average $950.89. White female reporters hired that year as fully experienced average $817.47. There were no black women hired that year who were rated as "fully experienced" under the contract. But then, there are only eight black female reporters out of a total reporting staff of 191, according to the Post's statistics.

If minimum salaries set by the contract were higher, it would result in more pay equity and in less freedom for the Post to set salaries arbitrarily — a freedom that has resulted in discrimination. At the New York Times, the key minimum is $929. At Newsday, it is $1,000. At the Washington Post it is a low $664.35, and if you are a black or a woman in a commercial or editorial job that earns the key minimum, your salary is likely to be much closer to that minimum than if you are a white male.

IF THE WASHINGTON POST IS SERIOUS ABOUT ELIMINATING DISCRIMINATION AT THE POST, IT WILL MOVE AWAY FROM THE MULTI-TIER SALARY SYSTEM.

— Martha Hamilton, for the Bargaining Committee
